etymology: American: from the literacy tests that exempted any man whose grandfather had voted - the exemption was the point and the test was the alibi.
effect: Keeps the existing practice legal while the new rule binds everyone who arrives after it, so the baseline never actually moves.
available_to: Any legislature that wants a reform to look larger than the number of people it covers.
counter: Date the exemption. A grandfather clause with an end date is a transition; one without is a permanent carve-out in a reform's clothes, and the difference is a line nobody reads.

confused_with.tell: The carve-out writes the exception into the rule; the grandfather clause writes the rule around what already exists.

senses: The legislative move that exempts what is already there: the rule applies to the future, the present keeps its permission, and the practice the rule was written about survives because it arrived first.

It works because transition relief is reasonable. Every real reform lets people finish what they started, and the grandfather clause arrives wearing that reason - when the transition ends is the only thing that separates the two, and that date is never in the text.
example: *"The **grandfather clause** exempted every plant already built, which was every plant, so the rule applied to a future that had not been scheduled."*
